title: Neetu Kapoor Plays a Grandmother Who Wants to Remarry — and It Just Landed on Netflix
excerpt: Ranbir's mum, Kapil Sharma, and the Kapoor family's quietest member Riddhima make a case for the most unexpectedly touching Punjabi family comedy of the year. Now streaming globally.
body:
The premise sounds like a joke at a kitty party — dadi wants to get married again, and the family loses its collective mind. But **Dadi Ki Shaadi**, which hits Netflix globally on July 3 after a theatrical run earlier this year, turns that setup into something warmer, messier, and more culturally pointed than the title suggests.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=vMYy2bNc9YU</youtube>

**Neetu Kapoor** plays the grandmother at the centre of the storm. She's luminous in it — and that word is chosen carefully, because at 67, Neetu Kapoor brings to this role the exact kind of grace that makes you understand why an entire joint family would simultaneously combust at the idea of her finding love again. It's not that she wants to be rebellious. It's that she wants to be happy. The family's problem isn't her happiness — it's that they never imagined she'd want it on her own terms.

**Kapil Sharma** plays Tony, her grandson, whose own wedding preparations are derailed the moment dadi makes her announcement. Sharma has been steadily building a film career alongside his television empire, and here he lands in comfortable territory — the loveable, slightly overwhelmed Punjabi man trying to hold a family together while it splinters around him. He's funny. He was always going to be funny. What's surprising is how grounded he is in the quieter moments.

But the real curiosity is **Riddhima Kapoor Sahni**, making her acting debut. Ranbir Kapoor's older sister, Rishi Kapoor's daughter, Neetu's real-life child — stepping onto a film set for the first time with her actual mother in the cast. The Kapoor family has never done anything small, and this particular piece of casting gives the film a layer of genuine tenderness that a different actress couldn't replicate.


> The title hints at a late-life wedding within a family. The idea itself brings a fresh angle — it opens space for humour and emotional moments.

Directed by **Ashish R Mohan** and produced by RTake Studios in association with BeingU Studios (co-founded by Kapil Sharma's wife **Ginni Chatrath**), the film is a Punjabi family comedy in the broadest sense — loud weddings, louder relatives, kitchen-table arguments, and the slow, painful process of watching an older generation assert its right to desire. The South Indian star **R. Sarathkumar** adds an unexpected cross-industry dimension to the cast, alongside **Sadia Khateeb** (who broke through in Shershaah) and veteran **Yograj Singh**.

The soundtrack is stacked: **Sonu Nigam**, **Sukhwinder Singh**, **Sunidhi Chauhan**, and **Rekha Bhardwaj** all lend their voices. For a family film about a grandmother's second innings, the music choices signal that the makers weren't treating this as a lightweight proposition.

## The Box Office Story

Dadi Ki Shaadi opened theatrically on May 8 to modest numbers — ₹0.60 crore on Day 1, climbing to ₹1.70 crore by its first Sunday, and settling around ₹4.90 crore net in its first week. Those aren't blockbuster numbers. But for a mid-budget family comedy without action sequences or franchise muscle, the film found its audience in multiplexes — particularly in Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad, and Chennai, where occupancy rates regularly crossed 30-40%.

The real play was always Netflix. The film carried the streaming giant's logo from its first poster, and the 56-day theatrical-to-OTT window was built into the business model from the start. For NRI families who never had a chance to see it in cinemas — and let's be honest, most Bollywood family comedies don't get wide international theatrical runs — Netflix is where this film will find its true audience.

## Why Diaspora Families Should Watch

Here's what the film gets right: the conversation it's having. A grandmother remarrying is still taboo in most Indian families, and doubly so in Punjabi households where widowhood carries a specific cultural weight. The film doesn't dodge that. It uses comedy as the way in — the family chaos, the wedding drama, the generational clash — but the emotional core is about a woman's right to a second chapter.

For diaspora viewers, particularly those navigating the space between Indian family expectations and Western ideas about individual happiness, Dadi Ki Shaadi hits a specific nerve. It's the kind of film you watch with your parents on a Saturday night and then spend an hour arguing about afterward. That's the highest compliment a family comedy can earn.

**Now streaming on Netflix worldwide.** Hindi audio. Subtitles available.
